analysis.one_liner: Restores federal pre-approval of state voting changes and strengthens protections against racial discrimination in voting.
analysis.headline: The voting rights bill was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Judiciary Committee, where it sat without a hearing or a single vote until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The John R. Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act would rebuild parts of the 1965 Voting Rights Act. It sets a new formula so that states and counties with repeated recent voting rights violations must get federal approval — from the Justice Department or a federal court — before putting certain voting changes into effect. It also makes it easier to sue over voting rules that make it harder for racial and language minority citizens to vote, requires public notice of election changes, and lets the Justice Department demand election records during investigations. The bill was introduced on the Senate floor with 49 cosponsors and immediately referred to the Judiciary Committee, which took no action on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters — particularly Black, Latino, Asian American, Native American, and other language-minority voters — who live in states or counties with records of voting discrimination. The bill would require those jurisdictions to pre-clear certain voting changes (new ID rules, polling place closures, redistricting plans, cuts to multilingual materials), lower the bar for courts to block discriminatory rules, and add public notice requirements so voters can see changes to polling places and districts before an election [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters of color and language minorities

how_it_helps.text: Sets a new formula under which states with 10 or more (at least one by the state itself) and political subdivisions with 3 or more voting rights violations in the previous 25 years are covered and must pre-clear voting changes for 10 years [S2].

Creates a second, practice-based pre-clearance trigger: any state or county must get approval before implementing specific changes — stricter voter ID or documentation rules, reductions in polling locations or voting hours (including Sunday voting), cuts to multilingual ballots, at-large election changes, and redistricting where a minority group's population has grown 20% or more — in areas where minority groups make up a significant share of the voting-age population [S2].

Restores the vote-dilution standard from Thornburg v. Gingles and lowers the bar to prove vote denial: a rule is unlawful if it imposes a discriminatory burden on a protected class linked to historical discrimination, even if the state's stated purpose is partly partisan [S2].

Requires public notice, on government websites, of changes to voting rules, polling place locations and resources, and district boundaries, with special accessibility formats for voters with disabilities [S2].

Gives the Attorney General power to demand election documents from states during voting rights investigations, expands who can sue (any 'aggrieved person'), and makes it harder for courts to deny relief close to an election, including a safe harbor for suits filed 45 or more days before an election [S2].
Provides federal grants to small jurisdictions (populations of 10,000 or less) to help pay for the required public notices [S2].

analysis.who_pays: States and local election offices with records of violations would bear the cost of pre-clearance filings, litigation, and new public-notice duties, and would lose the ability to change voting rules unilaterally. The Justice Department would take on new enforcement, investigation, and grant responsibilities at federal expense. States challenging the bill's approach would also face the loss of discretion the Supreme Court removed in 2013, which is the fight the bill was written to re-open.

drawbacks.text: The pre-clearance regime counts violations going back 25 years and applies retrogression rules to actions taken on or after January 1, 2021, meaning states could face federal review based partly on conduct that predates the bill [S2].

It centralizes significant power in the Attorney General, who can demand election documents from states and whose non-objection (or failure to object within 60 days) lets a voting change take effect [S2].

The Supreme Court in 2013 (Shelby County v. Holder) struck down the old coverage formula on the ground that it was based on outdated data; supporters of the bill's critics argue that a formula anchored in past violations still treats states unequally and that election rules should be set by states, not screened in Washington. The bill was written to answer that ruling, but the constitutional question would have been litigated again.

Pre-clearance and notice duties add administrative work for thousands of county election offices, though the bill softens this by making compliance voluntary for smaller jurisdictions and offering grants to jurisdictions with populations of 10,000 or less [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For voters in jurisdictions with documented records of discrimination, the protections are substantial: pre-clearance would catch discriminatory changes before they take effect rather than after years of litigation. The costs are real but mostly borne by election offices and state governments — more paperwork, possible delays for even neutral changes, and a much larger federal enforcement role — and the constitutional fight over whether Congress can base coverage on historical violations would have returned to the courts regardless.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Dick Durbin introduced the John R. Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act of 2024 on February 29, 2024, with 49 cosponsors — 46 Senate Democrats and 3 independents [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day [S4].
That referral was the bill's last action: the committee held no hearing or markup and the full Senate never considered it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].
No Republican signed on as a cosponsor; all 49 cosponsors were Democrats or independents [S3].

Predecessor versions of the same bill passed the House in an earlier Congress but were stopped in the Senate by Republican filibusters, which require 60 votes to move a bill forward; the last Senate cloture attempt on the combined voting rights package failed in November 2022.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State governments and officeholders who would have faced federal pre-approval of their voting changes keep full discretion over election rules, and senators opposed to the bill never had to cast a public vote on it because it never left committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States that kept discretion over voting rules

industries.note: The bill's failure preserves their ability to change voting rules, districts, and polling places without federal pre-approval or public-notice mandates. Voters in jurisdictions with records of discrimination lose the pre-clearance protection the bill would have restored.

The bill would have added notice, documentation, and possible pre-clearance duties for counties and municipalities, offset for the smallest jurisdictions by federal compliance grants and a voluntary-compliance rule for small offices.
